Today's editorials and columns examine India's financial sector, gender gaps in apprenticeships, UK-EU carbon-border rules, China's economic vulnerabilities and a book exploring Aligarh's history

India's exporters, particularly MSMEs, face growing compliance challenges as the UK and EU implement their Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) regulations. | Illustration : Binay Sinha

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 29 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page. 

 

India’s resilient growth needs a financial sector able to channel savings into investment, finance projects of every scale and expand insurance and pensions, today’s first editorial says. The economy grew 7.8 per cent in the first quarter, prompting the IMF to raise its annual forecast to 7 per cent, while banks’ gross non-performing loan ratio has fallen to 1.8 per cent. With global uncertainty affecting capital flows, the editorial urges the BFSI sector to mobilise domestic savings and calls for prompt action on concerns raised by foreign investors. Women’s growing participation in apprenticeships is not yet translating into equal access to skilled, better-paid work, the second editorial cautions. Women made up 29.5 per cent of NAPS apprentices in 2026-27, but only 6 per cent of electricians and 2.6 per cent of fitters; some technical trades had none. Training alone is insufficient: care burdens, unsafe travel, workplace conditions and limited job access constrain employment and advancement. The editorial calls for tracking completion, placements, wages and progression, alongside childcare, safe transport, affordable accommodation and effective grievance systems, so policy measures job quality as well as entry. Indian exporters need urgent support to meet the UK and EU carbon-border rules taking effect in 2027, writes Amita Batra. Although the UK recognises India’s carbon-credit system, many small and medium-sized firms lack the monitoring, verification and documentation needed to claim offsets; default emissions values could leave them facing higher charges. The EU’s more granular rules will also require detailed supply-chain data. Batra calls for product-code mapping, funding for emissions-accounting systems, training for exporters and alignment between Indian and European carbon-measurement frameworks to protect the market access offered by recent trade agreements. China faces a dangerous convergence of political succession risks, economic slowdown and weakening public finances, warn Navneeraj Sharma and Arvind Subramanian. The Communist Party has centralised power under Xi Jinping, while property woes, ageing and external trade pressures cloud growth. Its fiscal model is also strained: personal income tax has averaged just 1.2 per cent of GDP over the past decade, and taxes excluding social insurance fell from 18.4 per cent of GDP in 2012 to 12.6 per cent in 2025. The authors caution that even a gradual erosion of growth and state capacity could trigger another global shock. Atif Syed’s Aligarh: The City That Outlasted Empires traces the city’s layered history through archival records and overlooked connections. Saurabh Sharma appreciates Syed’s research, particularly his account of Aligarh’s French families and the city’s syncretic past, but finds much of the book a dry chronicle that may deter general readers. The early origin stories and chapters linking the past to places still present in the city offer more engaging moments. Sharma says the valuable discoveries needed a stronger narrative to make them more accessible.

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 28 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  The push to expand ethanol fuels and flex-fuel vehicles may reduce oil dependence and urban pollution, but India should slow the transition, says today's first editorial. E20 arrived five years ahead of schedule, and motorists report fuel-efficiency losses of 7–12 per cent, despite official claims of Rs 1.9 trillion in import savings and 31 million tonnes of crude substituted. Ethanol has supported farm incomes and rural jobs, but rising sugar prices underline food-security risks. Expanding water-intensive sugarcane and maize cultivation could also strain resources and damage ecosystems, as Brazil’s experience suggests.  Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election gives Brazil’s veteran left-wing president a chance to shape his legacy, but fiscal strains and hostile markets threaten his plans, the second editorial notes. Debt has risen from about 72 per cent to 83 per cent of GDP since 2022, while his spending pledges face legislative resistance to tax increases. Markets reacted sharply to his victory, with stocks and the real tumbling and bond yields surging. The editorial cautions that Lula may turn to geopolitics instead, positioning Brazil against Donald Trump’s Monroe doctrine and deepening its opposition to US influence. India should adapt its cybersecurity framework to artificial intelligence (AI)-driven threats by testing high-risk systems, measuring operational resilience and strengthening coordination among CERT-In and sectoral regulators, write Ajay Tyagi and Basu Chandola. Recent incidents involving Indian organisations and eMudhra show how AI can accelerate the exploitation of conventional vulnerabilities and how weaknesses may escape audits. The authors recommend clearer responsibilities for AI developers and deployers, shared testing standards and operational support from the IndiaAI Safety Institute. They say cyber governance must measure whether institutions can anticipate, contain and recover from attacks, rather than rely on procedural compliance alone. With just 3 per cent of global GDP but nearly a fifth of its population, India must build globally competitive businesses rather than rely on domestic demand, says Sachchidanand Shukla. He says US tariffs are pushing exporters towards higher-value manufacturing, research and development, innovation and overseas investment. Refining, pharmaceuticals, clean energy, electronics and specialised services show how firms are adapting, while exports and market destinations diversify. But trade pressure alone will not create competitiveness: India must cut logistics costs, provide predictable regulation and reliable infrastructure, deepen skills and widen access to patient capital. The goal, Shukla says, is to trade volume for value and build capabilities the world cannot easily replace. The 21 days before independence emerge as a tense contest to keep princely states from breaking up India in Josy Joseph’s Birth of a Nation: The Twenty-One Days that Made India. Sneha Pathak praises Joseph’s archival research and thriller-like account of the “faceless civil servants” and palace spies who helped secure the Union. The shifting narrative conveys the States Department’s urgency, though the book ends before some crises are resolved. Nonetheless, Pathak calls it an absorbing, meticulously-researched read.

entry.title: Choices between worthy goals pulling in different directions
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Choices between worthy goals pulling in different directionsChoices between worthy goals pulling in different directions

Good policy lies in balancing competing priorities, from affordability and innovation to inclusion and protection, while ensuring growth, accountability and long-term sustainability

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Reetesh Anand New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTGood policy is not so much about a choice between right and wrong as it is between two worthwhile goals pulling in different directions. Health care must be affordable, but innovation needs incentives. Credit should be easier to access, but data and borrowers need protection. Domestic investors can support markets, but global competitiveness still matters. Boards must supervise without micromanaging. Businesses can pursue purpose, but they cannot ignore economic viability. The difficulty begins when both objectives are legitimate. Our first editorial today, “Pricing pain points”, looks at health care price controls. The impulse to make treatment more affordable is understandable, especially in a country where out-of-pocket medical spending remains high. But blunt price intervention can create unintended consequences by weakening incentives for companies to launch new medicines, invest in innovation or supply products sustainably. The challenge is to improve affordability without undermining the economics that make better treatment possible. Access matters, but so does the capacity to keep producing what patients need. The second editorial, “Seamless credit network”, looks at interoperable digital lending. Better sharing of financial information can make credit more accessible, particularly for borrowers who are poorly served by traditional banking. But greater connectivity also raises questions about consent, privacy, data security, responsible lending and competition. Inclusion cannot come at the cost of weaker safeguards. A credit network becomes genuinely useful only when convenience and protection advance together. In “Risk of irrelevance?”, Akash Prakash talks about the tension in Indian equities. Domestic investors have supported the market even as foreign investors have sold heavily. That is a source of strength, but it should not become a reason to dismiss prolonged underperformance or declining international interest. India still needs to remain attractive to global capital. A deeper domestic investor base can reduce dependence on foreign flows, but it cannot substitute for earnings growth, competitive valuations and confidence in India’s long-term economic prospects. Rama Bijapurkar’s column, “Uneasy lies the governance space”, examines the boundary between boards and management. Boards are meant to challenge, oversee and protect shareholder interests, but not to run the company. Management needs enough freedom to operate effectively, but it cannot be allowed to escape scrutiny. Trouble begins when oversight turns into interference or autonomy turns into unaccountability. Good governance depends on keeping that boundary clear. M S Sriram’s review of Eric Ries’ Incorruptible, “The double-edged sword of a dual bottom line”, confronts the tension between profit and purpose. Organisations that pursue both commercial returns and social objectives can create powerful models, but they also face competing incentives and difficult accountability questions. The hardest systems, these pieces show, are not those with one goal. They are those with two good ones. Success depends on knowing where the balance lies.

entry.title: Best of Business Standard Opinion: Resilience comes from widening the base
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Business Standard Opinion: Resilience comes from widening the baseBest of Business Standard Opinion: Resilience comes from widening the base

Even knowledge systems are stronger when authority is distributed rather than concentrated

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Reetesh Anand3 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTYou can’t build resilience by putting everything behind one answer. A household that leans too heavily on gold-backed borrowing becomes vulnerable to asset prices. An investor who treats an entire sector as one trade can miss differences between firms. A country that relies on a single policy tool to manage external stress discovers its limits. Agriculture becomes more fragile when crop diversity narrows. Even knowledge systems are stronger when authority is distributed rather than concentrated. “Glitter of gold loans”, our first editorial today, looks at the rapid growth of household borrowing against gold. Gold is convenient collateral and gives lenders security, which explains why these loans are popular. But the editorial warns that the pace of expansion deserves scrutiny. When household borrowing rises alongside high gold prices, apparent comfort can conceal underlying stress. A strong collateral asset does not eliminate repayment risk, and excessive dependence on gold-backed credit can become a vulnerability if household finances weaken or asset prices reverse.  The second editorial, “Value buying”, looks at Indian IT sector. Artificial intelligence is reshaping this sector, changing client spending and causing company strategies to diverge. That makes blanket sector calls less useful. Investors need to look more closely at productivity, adaptability, valuations, client exposure and each company’s ability to navigate technological change. Indian IT is no longer one homogeneous bet; resilience in investing comes from distinguishing between firms rather than treating the sector as a single trade. In “Ten rules for external sector stress”, Ajay Shah, K P Krishnan and G Padmanabhan make the diversification argument more directly. External shocks cannot be managed through one instrument, whether that is defending the rupee, using reserves or tightening monetary policy. Exchange-rate flexibility, fiscal discipline, banking resilience, capital flows, reserves and institutional credibility all have a role. The lesson from past episodes of stress is to maintain several lines of defence rather than place excessive faith in any one of them. Surinder Sud’s column, “The neglected species of pulses”, brings the theme to agriculture. India’s focus on a relatively small group of major pulses has left many traditional varieties underused. Yet these crops can offer nutritional benefits, suit different agroclimatic conditions and improve resilience to climate stress. A more diverse crop basket can strengthen both food security and farm resilience. “Wikipedia’s origin story, warts and all”, Jennifer Szalai’s review of Richard Cooke’s The Last Best Place on the Internet, turns to knowledge. Wikipedia grew by distributing the creation and correction of information across a vast community rather than concentrating authority among a small editorial elite. That openness created governance problems of its own, but it also made the platform unusually adaptive. Resilience, as we see across all these pieces, comes from widening the base — spreading risk and avoiding dependence on a single answer.

entry.title: The neglected species of pulses
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The neglected species of pulsesThe neglected species of pulses

Reviving neglected pulses could boost nutrition, reduce imports and improve farmers' incomes

premium

Underutilised pulses could strengthen India’s nutritional security while supporting farmers and reducing import dependence

Surinder Sud5 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 10:46 PM ISTIn a country where pulses (dal) are the major source of protein for most people, malnutrition is rampant, and import dependence for meeting pulses requirements is substantial, the suboptimal utilisation of the existing diversity of indigenous legumes is hard to justify. Only eight of the available 14 species of pulses are grown and consumed on a regular basis. The others (leguminous crops) have either been abandoned or are cultivated and consumed in specific areas on a small scale. Many of these underexploited species have impressive nutritional profiles. Their mainstreaming can be a boon to consumers, as also to small and marginal farmers, who have traditionally been growing these hardy and drought-resistant crops in arid, semi-arid, and degraded lands, but have stopped doing so because of waning market demand.  These underutilised species include Moth bean (Moth dal), Lathyrus (Khesari dal), Horse gram (Kulthi), Faba bean (Bakla or Kala matar), Rice bean (Sutri or Lal bean), and Adzuki bean (Lal mung or Lal chowri). Their farming is confined to limited areas, chiefly for local consumption. Going by their merits, in terms of versatility, ease of cultivation, and health benefits, these deserve better usage.  Unfortunately, these species of pulses have been neglected even by agricultural scientists and are, therefore, often dubbed as “orphan crops”. Not enough research & development has been done to improve their productivity, grain quality, processability, and marketability by developing superior high-yielding crop strains. Such apathy towards these valuable legumes is unwarranted, given the dire need to augment the availability of protein-dense foods to strengthen nutritional security.  The country’s pulses sector is dominated by just five legumes, which together account for 90 per cent of production and consumption. These are pigeon pea (tur or arhar), chickpea (chana or gram), green gram (mung), black gram (urad), and lentil (masoor). The bulk of the remaining 10 per cent consumption is shared by three pulses – red kidney beans (Rajma), black eyed peas (Lobiya), and field peas (Matar).  There are, indeed, several good reasons for harnessing the untapped potential of the little-used pulses. For one, these can boost the domestic supply of legumes to reduce pulses imports, which amounted to 7 million tonnes in 2024-25 and 6 million tonnes in 2025-26. Besides, these pulses can grow on poor-quality lands not ideally suited for cultivating main cereals and commercial crops. In fact, being leguminous crops, these can improve the fertility of such lands by fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil. These crops can, therefore, serve virtually as an effective means of regenerating degraded lands, which abound in India, spanning over 98 million hectares. Moreover, these crops, requiring little investment in cash inputs, can be a vital livelihood support for resource-starved farmers owning such lands. And most importantly, they are regarded by farm scientists as a repository of genes that might prove useful in imparting climate change-resilience, immunity against diseases and pests, and other desirable traits, in future crop species.  Interestingly, most of these underexploited crops possess significant amounts of dietary fibre and bioactive compounds, which can mitigate the challenges posed by the rising incidence of lifestyle and flawed nutrition-induced ailments, such as diabetes, hypertension, obesity, cardiovascular diseases, and even cancer.  The reasons for these species of pulses falling out of favour, though formidable, are not difficult to overcome. Many of their drawbacks can be remedied through simple treatment and managerial intervention, such as soaking in water or processing them into value-added products to prepare nutritious snacks. In the case of Moth bean, for instance, the main problem is the long time it takes to cook. This can easily be cut down to half by soaking the grains in water overnight. Preparing in a pressure cooker can reduce it further.  The Khesari dal, which has a very high protein content of 26-28 per cent, was temporarily banned because of the rise in the incidence of neurological disorder called lathyrism (paralysis of lower limbs) among its regular consumers in regions like Bihar, Jharkhand and eastern Uttar Pradesh. Scientific studies later revealed that this condition was caused due to the presence of a neurotoxin, called beta-ODAP, in Khesari dal, and affected primarily those who ate this cheapest available legume almost as a staple. Studies also showed that the problem could be largely solved by soaking it in salt water, and discarding the water. This lowers the toxin level down to almost safe limits, especially if consumed in moderation.  Sprouting is another simple and effective way of improving the digestibility of these less used pulses, and also their acceptability among people. It activates their internal enzymes, which transform these grains into nutritional powerhouses.  There is, thus, a strong case for making better use of the underexploited legumes to enhance the overall availability of pulses. The Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses, set up last year to make the country self-sufficient in pulses by 2030-31, would hopefully do the needful in this direction.
